strengths: Significance: Reducing expensive target-gradient queries using cheaper auxiliary information is a useful optimization problem. The framework connects batch reuse, transfer learning, and federated optimization, with potential value when target gradients are costly.

Originality: Allowing an arbitrary auxiliary objective offers a useful unifying perspective on control-variate methods. Hessian similarity can accommodate substantially different gradients and minimizers, which is an interesting conceptual contribution.

Soundness of motivation: The shifted-quadratic example in Appendix C.1 convincingly illustrates why uncorrected auxiliary updates can remain biased even when the target and auxiliary Hessians coincide.

Presentation and reproducibility: Equation (1) explains the correction intuitively. Appendix A provides the network architecture, batch sizes, learning-rate schedules, and a code URL; the detailed proof appendix enables scrutiny.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript appropriately acknowledges the absence of test-performance guarantees and the additional weak-convexity requirement for averaging multiple helpers. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent from the reported methods.
weaknesses: Soundness, decisive: Theorem 4.2 is false with its stated parameter choices. It sets a = 32LKη, whereas Lemma 9's proof requires 0 < a ≤ 1. Consider deterministic f(x) = h(x) = x²/2, L = K = 1, δ = 1/192, and x⁰ = m⁰ = 1. The prescribed noiseless tuning gives η = 1 and a = 32. AuxMom then produces x¹ = 0, x² = 31, x³ = −1922, and diverges, contradicting the claimed O(1/T) bound. Corrected tuning and a proof preserving the claimed acceleration are necessary.

Further theoretical inconsistencies require resolution. Assumption 3 bounds the squared Hessian norm by 2δ, but Lemma 4 uses a δ² bound on squared gradient increments; these are not equivalent for small δ. Theorem 4.2 has K under the noise-dependent stepsize radical, whereas the derivation on page 17 has K². Theorem 4.3 also omits the enlarged initial batch and zero initial displacement used on page 22. These discrepancies affect the assumptions and executable prescriptions behind the guarantees.

Evaluation and significance: Figures 1–3 compare choices of K against iteration counts without reporting elapsed time, total gradient-evaluation cost, or comparisons at matched computational budgets. Increasing K adds auxiliary work. In the noisy regression experiment, both target and helper batches have size one, so auxiliary cheapness is not demonstrated. The curves suggest improvement per round but do not establish computational speedups over appropriately budgeted SGD or variance-reduction baselines.

Applicability: Assumption 3 requires similarity for every stochastic auxiliary sample, but the compressed-model discussion on page 6 checks only a mask-averaged Hessian condition. That weaker condition does not justify the theorem for randomly sampled masks. The experiments also do not measure δ or investigate the tradeoff between auxiliary cost and similarity, leaving the practically useful regime insufficiently characterized.

Originality: The paper acknowledges close connections to MiMeSGDm, MiMeMVR, SVRG, and DANE, but does not precisely isolate the new guarantees relative to these methods under matched assumptions and oracle costs. The unifying interpretation has merit, while the extent of the claimed algorithmic and theoretical advance remains insufficiently established.

Presentation and reproducibility: The regression dataset is unnamed and its provenance is unspecified. Experimental reporting omits which proposed variant generated the plots, the momentum parameter a, initialization, tuning procedures, seed counts, and uncertainty estimates. The MVR description also contains ambiguous initialization and local-step indexing. The code URL helps, but the manuscript needs a consistent algorithm specification and fuller experimental documentation.
